query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting Ta with Nb in HfMoTaTiZr (to form HfMoNbTiZr) will reduce the alloy’s density while preserving its high strength and single-phase microstructure at both room temperature and up to approximately 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr with a density of ~10.21 g/cm³, exhibiting a single-phase BCC solid solution and high mechanical strength at room and elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Replace the Ta element with Nb in the alloy composition, creating an as-cast HfMoNbTiZr alloy.
generation.conditions: The alloy should perform under typical mechanical loading conditions (e.g., tensile or compressive tests) across a temperature range from room temperature up to approximately 1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of the single-phase BCC solid solution structure and lattice distortion effects (solid-solution strengthening) that characterize the refractory high-entropy alloy.
generation.mechanism: Nb has a lower atomic weight than Ta yet maintains comparable refractory characteristics and similar atomic radii. This substitution is expected to lower the overall density while preserving the key lattice distortion and diffusion sluggishness mechanisms responsible for the alloy’s strength at both room temperature and elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable decrease in alloy density relative to 10.21 g/cm³ with minimal or no loss in mechanical properties (yield strength and phase stability) at room temperature and near 1000 °C, maintaining a single-phase BCC structure.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties and single-phase microstructure of the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy at room temperature and at approximately 1000 °C.
generation.boundary: Temperature range: Room temperature to about 1000 °C; Loading conditions: standard tensile/compressive/mechanical tests typical for high-strength refractory alloys.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the exact magnitude of the performance retention post-substitution, as minor changes in solid-solution strengthening parameters or phase stability could occur. Further experimental validation is required.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the as-cast HfMoNbTiZr alloy using the same processing parameters as used for HfMoTaTiZr. Characterize the alloy’s density using standard methods, perform phase analysis (e.g., XRD and TEM) to confirm the retention of a single-phase BCC structure, and conduct mechanical testing (tensile or compressive tests) at room temperature and at approximately 1000 °C.
measurements: Tensile/compressive yield strength and ductility at room temperature and ~1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the Nb substitution does not result in a significant density decrease compared to 10.21 g/cm³, or if the alloy shows a substantial reduction in mechanical strength or phase stability (e.g., formation of secondary phases or brittle intermetallic compounds) at room temperature or near 1000 °C.

cited_evidence.text: There are some researches working on the addition of Al [,], Mo [], Ti [], V [], or Zr [], but few of them focus on the elevated-temperature mechanical performance and the overall effect of the constituent elements. To understand the elemental effect on mechanical properties, equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy is firstly designed as a base alloy by adding the high modulus refractory element Mo to HfNbTaTiZr. Then the subtraction method is used to analyze each elemental effect in the equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr. Thus, in this study, six alloys HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi are investigated and compared on their microstructure. Further, the compressive properties at room temperature and at elevated temperature are investigated. By comparing HfMoNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr, the influence of the addition of Mo can be understood. Likewise, the influence of the addition of Nb, Ta, Ti, or Zr can be articulated. In addition, promising compositions were found and further improved design is suggested. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solid solution strengthening effect will be discussed.

frame.system: The starting material is an as‐cast refractory high‐entropy alloy with composition HfMoTaTiZr that exhibits a single-phase microstructure with high strength at room and elevated temperatures but a high density (10.21 g/cm³).
frame.goal: Reduce the alloy’s overall density while preserving its excellent mechanical performance at room temperature and at high temperatures (up to approximately 1000 °C).
frame.limitation: The alloy’s high density limits its application despite its superior strength and high‐temperature stability.
root_cause_cues: without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures
constraints: A single intervention (i.e., only one compositional change)
Preservation of mechanical properties at both room temperature and ~1000 °C
Must be applicable to the as‐cast state
frame.regime: The material is intended to perform under tensile/compressive or similar mechanical loads at room temperature and in the high-temperature regime around 1000 °C.
prior_attempts: The as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr composition itself already provides high strength at room and elevated temperatures, but no previous intervention has resolved the high density issue without affecting these properties.
frame.understanding: The proposed mechanism is that substituting the heaviest constituent element with a lighter but compositionally similar refractory metal will reduce the overall alloy density. In this case, replacing Ta—the element largely contributing to the high density due to its high atomic weight—with Nb, which has a lower density while offering comparable atomic radii and refractory behavior, could maintain the lattice distortion and solid-solution strengthening mechanisms. The expectation is that replacing Ta with Nb will lower the density while keeping the phase stability and the high-temperature mechanical strength intact.

proposal.intervention: Substitute Ta with Nb, i.e., develop an alloy variant HfMoNbTiZr.
proposal.mechanism: Nb’s lower atomic weight relative to Ta will reduce the overall density. Because Nb and Ta are chemically and physically similar (with comparable atomic radii and refractory characteristics), the alloy should maintain its single-phase structure and strength-enhancing lattice distortion, ensuring that mechanical performance at room temperature and up to ~1000 °C is preserved.

directional_changes.mechanical_properties: Maintain high strength at room temperature and high temperature (around 1000 °C)
directional_changes.microstructure: Retention of a stable single-phase solid solution, preserving diffusion sluggishness and lattice distortion effects

applicable_boundaries.loading: Mechanical loading conditions relevant for high-strength alloys (e.g., tensile/compressive tests)

proposal.supporting_prior_evidence: Studies in refractory high-entropy alloys have demonstrated that Nb-based alloys can exhibit high-temperature mechanical stability and strength comparable to Ta-containing alloys. Additionally, the close chemical similarity between Nb and Ta has been leveraged in prior alloy design to achieve density reductions without severe compromises in performance.
proposal.experimental_proposal: Prepare the as-cast HfMoNbTiZr alloy using similar processing parameters as the original alloy. Characterize its density, microstructure (e.g., phase analysis using XRD and TEM), and perform mechanical tests (e.g., tensile, compression, or hardness tests) at room temperature and at ~1000 °C. Compare these results directly with the original HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
proposal.rejection_criterion: If the substitution results in a significant deterioration of the mechanical properties (e.g., decreased yield strength or loss of high-temperature phase stability) or if the alloy displays phase decomposition or formation of brittle intermetallic phases at room temperature or near 1000 °C, the hypothesis would be falsified.

decision.trend: Early work on refractory high‐entropy alloys was focused on achieving excellent high‐temperature strength and room‐temperature ductility in as‐cast single‐phase alloys such as HfMoTaTiZr. Researchers then increasingly applied subtraction methods to isolate the role of individual elements (e.g., comparing alloys with and without Nb or Ta) to understand how each constituent influences phase stability and mechanical performance. In this progression, it was observed that heavy elements like Ta contribute significantly to density, while Nb, being lighter yet chemically similar, has been shown to maintain (or even improve) high‐temperature strength when substituted in similar alloy systems. The success in preserving desirable microstructure and strength in related systems has been encouraging, but the density reduction while retaining performance at both room temperature and up to ~1000 °C remains an unsolved limitation in HfMoTaTiZr.
decision.unsolved: The challenge remains to reduce the alloy’s high density (10.21 g/cm³) without compromising its well-established mechanical properties at both room temperature and elevated temperatures (~1000 °C).
decision.why: Following the trend observed in subtraction studies of refractory HEAs, replacing Ta with Nb in HfMoTaTiZr is a logical next step because Nb’s lower atomic weight is expected to reduce the overall density while its chemical and physical similarity with Ta helps maintain the lattice distortion and solid-solution strengthening mechanisms that underpin the alloy’s high-temperature performance. Prior evidence in related compositions supports the viability of this substitution as a strategy to alleviate the density issue.
